archetype.name: Point Guard (Shanahan timing distributor)
archetype.definition: A rhythm passer who wins by getting the ball out on schedule to Kittle, McCaffrey, Evans and Samuel underneath and over the middle, then punishes defenses that squeeze the short game with well-timed shots and second-reaction scrambles.

report.headline: His 2023 efficiency is back, but the protection under him just broke.
report.take:
Purdy is the same quarterback he has always been at his best: accurate, on time and ruthless with the layup throws Shanahan builds for him. His 0.329 EPA per dropback ranks 2nd of 55, his 9.05 yards per attempt ranks 2nd, and his 7.48 CPOE ranks 4th. That is a near-copy of his 2023 season, when he led the league at 0.338 EPA per play. The engine is the short game. On 134 throws under 10 air yards past the line he is completing 81.3% at 0.443 EPA, with 14 of his 23 touchdowns, and his throws over the middle (0.564 EPA, 9.7 CPOE) are the cleanest part of the field. This isn't a passer living on chunk plays. The offense ranks 1st in EPA and success rate, and he is the reason it moves.

What is different from last year is ball security and one new receiver. Interceptions are down to 0.5 a game from 1.11, even though his bad-throw rate is slightly up (12.8%, 16th of 45). Mike Evans has turned into the vertical answer this offense had lacked: 0.893 EPA per target on 47 targets, more total EPA than Kittle and McCaffrey, who see more of the ball. His deep passing (0.9 EPA and a 13.2 CPOE on 25 attempts of 20+ yards) and his red-zone line (16 TDs, no picks, 16.6 CPOE) are the two numbers carrying the headline stats. Both are real skills in a strong system, and both rest on samples small enough to cool off.

The last three games have been his best stretch: 0.512 EPA per dropback, 11.09 yards per attempt and a 12.4 CPOE. The 255-yard, 17.5-EPA game against Minnesota, today's top-ranked defense, says it isn't only the Raiders and Cowboys. The warning sign sits in the same window. His sack rate is 8.1% over those three games, 3.5 points above his season mark, with five sacks in Dallas. Now right-side starter Colton McKivitz, on the field for 93% of snaps, is done for the year with a fractured ankle. Purdy holds the ball (3.01 seconds to throw) and leans on extended plays: 21 scrambles at 0.802 EPA each, 13 of them moving the chains. So pass protection is the variable that matters most for the rest of his season.

strengths.title: Surgical short and middle game
strengths.body: Shanahan's timing concepts and yards-after-catch backs and tight ends make the short area his most reliable source of value. He is completing 81% there with a 9.2 CPOE, and throws over the middle grade even better. This has held across his career, so it is skill and scheme, not a hot streak.

strengths.title: Top-tier efficiency, backed by 2023
strengths.body: He ranks 2nd in EPA per dropback and 2nd in yards per attempt. His completion rate sits 8.9 points over the league average. The 2023 line (1st in EPA per play) shows this ceiling isn't new. With his best receiver group yet, efficiency near this level is sustainable.

strengths.title: Scrambles that pay for the hold
strengths.body: His 3.01-second time to throw costs some sacks, but the scrambles more than cover it: 0.802 EPA per scramble and 13 first downs on 21 tries. His designed runs do almost nothing (1.67 yards a carry), so the rushing value is improvised, not schemed.

concerns.title: Losing a starting tackle mid-surge
concerns.body: McKivitz played 93% of snaps and is out for the season. Purdy's recent sack rate was already climbing, and he took five sacks against a Dallas defense that ranks last. A quarterback who extends plays behind a weakened right side will take more hits, and his worst game this year came when he was pressured on 35% of dropbacks.

concerns.title: Deep and red-zone rates will cool
concerns.body: A 0.9 EPA on 25 deep attempts and 16 red-zone touchdowns with no interceptions are excellent, but they are small samples running above even his own career norms. Evans' 0.893 EPA per target is carrying much of it. Expect fewer touchdowns per game rather than a collapse.

concerns.title: Intermediate window is where picks live
concerns.body: Three of his five interceptions came on 10-19 yard throws, where he completes just 57.8%. His bad-throw rate is middle of the pack. The ball-security gain over last year is partly luck that this range could give back.

trend.note: A sluggish middle stretch (Seattle, Washington, Atlanta) gave way to his three best games of the year. Efficiency in the last three sits 0.183 EPA per dropback above his season mark, but the sack rate has risen alongside it.

nextGame.headline: Seattle's deep-ball lockdown meets a line missing its right tackle
nextGame.body:
Seattle is the one defense that has truly beaten Purdy this year. In Week 5 he was pressured on 35.3% of dropbacks and finished at -0.1 passing EPA. This unit ranks 1st in success rate, 3rd in pass EPA and 1st against deep passes. It allows the fewest yards per game to quarterbacks. The opening is underneath: Seattle ranks 25th against short throws. That is exactly where Purdy does most of his damage, so expect a quick-game, middle-of-the-field plan rather than Evans shot plays.

Availability cuts both ways. McKivitz's loss lands right before a front that ranks 4th in hit rate and 9th in sack rate. Seattle is missing DT Leonard Williams, with Jarran Reed questionable, which softens the interior rush somewhat. On the other side, Seattle's offense is in rough shape: Darnold is listed out with a quadriceps injury (though he suited up for an unofficial practice), Nelson and Cross are out, and Lucas is questionable. That favors a controlled 49ers lead and the Book's SF -3, but it also leans toward a lower-volume, run-heavier day for Purdy.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Seattle gives up 0.075 EPA on short throws while erasing deep ones. Purdy's 0.443 EPA on short attempts is his bread and butter, so the matchup funnels him into his strength.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's pass rush vs. new tackle
keyMatchups.body: Seattle hits quarterbacks at one of the league's highest rates. The first meeting was Purdy's most-pressured game of the season and his only negative-EPA outing. A backup at McKivitz's spot makes a repeat plausible unless the plan is built around quick throws.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Seattle offense shapes script
keyMatchups.body: With their quarterback and two starting linemen out, Seattle may struggle to force a shootout. A lead likely means more McCaffrey and fewer dropbacks, capping volume even if efficiency holds.

nextGame.watch: How fast the ball comes out on early downs: under 3 seconds and heavy middle-of-the-field targeting means Shanahan is protecting the new tackle; long-developing shots to Evans mean sack risk.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable: a top-ranked offense, a varied set of targets and a short-area game that has held across his career. Expect him to keep ranking near the top in efficiency. What regresses is the edge. The deep EPA, the red-zone touchdown rate and Evans' per-target value are all running hot on modest samples. A touchdown pace near 2.3 a game is more likely to settle around two. The bigger swing is protection. His sack rate has already climbed, and McKivitz's absence for the rest of the year makes it likely to stay up, especially against good front sevens.

Volume is the quiet limiter. He averages 29 attempts in a team that wins, so blowouts like Minnesota trim his counting stats. Expect roughly 240-280 yards in competitive games and less when the 49ers control the script, with scramble yardage adding a steady floor.
swingFactors: Who replaces McKivitz and how the sack rate responds

confidence.note: Ten starts and a strong career baseline, but a new line hole and small deep and red-zone samples.
